Normalize an Objective for the Optimizers

Source: R/objective.R
as_objective.Rd

Packs a function to be minimized, together with its gradient and Hessian when the caller has them, into the handle on which every algorithm in the package operates. The result is a named list that contains the pieces and two flags recording which derivatives were supplied. as_objective() is a generic that dispatches on fn, so a caller with another kind of objective registers one method and every algorithm accepts that objective.

Usage

as_objective(fn, gr = NULL, he = NULL, ...)

Arguments

fn

The objective, a function of the parameter vector returning a single number to be minimized. An object of some other class is accepted whenever a method has been registered for it; without one, dispatch fails and reports the class that it was handed.

gr

The gradient, a function of the parameter vector returning a numeric vector of the same length. NULL, the default, has the gradient differenced from fn as above. Any other value is an error.

he

The Hessian, a function of the parameter vector returning a p x p symmetric matrix. NULL is the default. newton() and chebyshev() read it; every other method accepts it and does not use it, so calling code can pass whatever it has without branching on the method.

...

Passed to the method that dispatch selects. The shipped method for an ordinary function does not read it.

Value

A named list of six components describing the objective to the compiled side:

kind

character, "r" for an ordinary R function.

fn

the objective as supplied.

gr

the gradient, or NULL.

he

the Hessian, or NULL.

has_gradient

logical, whether gr was supplied.

has_hessian

logical, whether he was supplied.

Dispatch of the two generics

minimize() dispatches on the optimizer, so an algorithm is written once for every kind of objective. as_objective() dispatches on the objective, so each kind of objective is converted once for every algorithm. Dispatching minimize() on both would need one method for each pair of an algorithm and a kind of objective. The package ships one method, for an ordinary R function.

A gradient obtained by differencing

The compiled loop differences the objective, once per coordinate, $$\hat{g}_j = \frac{f(x + h e_j) - f(x - h e_j)}{2h}, \qquad h = \varepsilon^{1/3} \max(1, \lvert x_j \rvert),$$ with \(\varepsilon\) the machine epsilon, so \(h\) is about 6.06e-06 for a coordinate of size one. One gradient then costs \(2p\) evaluations of the objective, and its relative error is of the order of \(\varepsilon^{2/3}\).

A run that differences its gradient records this in the message field of the result.

A Hessian by differencing the gradient

newton() and chebyshev() read a Hessian, and the Hessian is obtained by differencing the gradient once when the caller does not supply one. With an analytic gradient this is a single differentiation and costs \(2p\) gradient evaluations. Without a gradient, the gradient is itself a difference and the Hessian is a difference of differences, which costs about \(4p^2\) evaluations of the objective and is less accurate. The Hessian is symmetrized before it is returned, since its two triangles differ by the error of the differences.

Points where the objective is not finite

If the objective returns NA, NaN or an infinity at a point other than the starting value, the algorithms treat that point as unusable, reject the trial step and continue, so a line search can try points outside the region where the objective is defined. A value that is not finite at the starting value is an error.

See also

minimize() for the run itself, newton() and chebyshev() for the methods that read a Hessian, optimizer_provides() for the quantities that a method supplies to a stopping rule.

Examples

# The flags record what was supplied, and the compiled loop branches on them.
str(as_objective(function(p) sum(p^2)))
#> List of 6
#>  $ kind        : chr "r"
#>  $ fn          :function (p)  
#>  $ gr          : NULL
#>  $ he          : NULL
#>  $ has_gradient: logi FALSE
#>  $ has_hessian : logi FALSE
str(as_objective(function(p) sum(p^2), gr = function(p) 2 * p))
#> List of 6
#>  $ kind        : chr "r"
#>  $ fn          :function (p)  
#>  $ gr          :function (p)  
#>  $ he          : NULL
#>  $ has_gradient: logi TRUE
#>  $ has_hessian : logi FALSE

# The example measures the cost of the difference on Rosenbrock from the
# origin. Both runs take
# 21 iterations and reach the same point; the evaluation counts differ.
f <- function(p) (1 - p[1])^2 + 100 * (p[2] - p[1]^2)^2
g <- function(p) c(-2 * (1 - p[1]) - 400 * p[1] * (p[2] - p[1]^2),
                   200 * (p[2] - p[1]^2))

a <- minimize(bfgs(), f, c(0, 0))
b <- minimize(bfgs(), f, c(0, 0), gr = g)
unlist(a@counts)          # 126 objective evaluations, no gradients
#>   f   g   h 
#> 126   0   0 
unlist(b@counts)          # 30 objective evaluations and 24 gradients
#>  f  g  h 
#> 30 24  0 
max(abs(a@par - b@par))   # the two answers agree to 1.5e-08
#> [1] 1.466677e-08

# The message of the run that differenced records it.
a@message
#> [1] "gradient obtained by finite differences"

# A class with no method is rejected, and the error names the class.
try(as_objective(1:3))
#> Error : Can't find method for `as_objective(<integer>)`.
